name: VPN, proxy and Tor detection
plain: Sites guess whether the visitor hides behind a VPN, proxy or Tor.
meaning: Methods: IP lists (Tor exit list, hosting ASNs), latency versus claimed geography, timezone and language versus IP, WebRTC leaks, open ports, MTU and TCP quirks. Residential VPN IPs often slip through.

web.api: IP reputation; Tor bulk exit list; RTT triangulation; timezone mismatch

steps: Compare IP geo with timezone and Accept-Language
Measure latency and run WebRTC probe

fields.name: is_vpn
fields.precision: vendor score, false positives about 1 to 10%

limits.headline: Can guess whether you are hiding behind a VPN, proxy or Tor, but not always correctly
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when you load a page, sign in, or watch video
can: Check your address against lists of VPN, hosting and Tor addresses
Compare your timezone and language with where your address seems to be
Spot slow response times that suggest a faraway server
Block or challenge you, or show a different catalog
cannot: Be sure when you use a home internet VPN address, which often slips through
Learn your real address if the VPN holds up
See your name or account from detection alone
Avoid wrongly flagging people who use privacy tools for safety

story.what_it_is: Sites guess if you are hiding behind a VPN, proxy or Tor, using address lists and timing clues.
story.for_you: You may see a block page, a missing video or extra checks, and no clear reason. The site thinks your address belongs to a VPN, a data center or Tor, so it treats you with caution.
story.for_makers: Makers buy lists of VPN, proxy and Tor addresses to enforce region rules, stop fraud and slow bots. It is a blunt tool. It also catches honest people who use a VPN for privacy.

use_cases.example: Streaming sites such as Netflix and BBC iPlayer block known VPN addresses to enforce regional licenses, so a viewer abroad sees a proxy error.
A game's store checks for VPN use at purchase to stop regional price tricks, and may ask for a card from the local country.
A bank asks for extra proof when a login arrives from Tor or a known proxy, which may lock out a traveler.
A checkout page scores VPN traffic as higher risk and holds the first order for review.
An ad network refuses to bill clicks from data center and proxy addresses, because they are mostly bots.
A social site restricts new accounts from Tor to slow spam, though a journalist in a risky country may need Tor.
A ticket queue blocks proxy addresses so one buyer cannot hold many places in line.

technical_bounds: False positives on corporate and school networks
Residential proxies and private relays are hard to flag
